name: Pedro Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a continuous miner at the Brennan potash mine, a kilometre down. It's a big machine with a spinning drum on the front that cuts the ore straight out of the wall and loads it onto a conveyor. I'm on a four-on, four-off roster, twelve-hour shifts. The good part is when the cut goes clean and you hit your metres for the shift, and the bad part is the dust in the filters and the back pain on the drive home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life outside the mine.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my fiancée, Marta, in a rented semi in Hollin, about forty minutes from the mine. She's a teaching assistant at the primary school. We got engaged in the spring and we're trying to save for the wedding, but honestly we've got less than a month of bills in the bank. I'm on the lower end of the pay scale because the union deal only lifts you after five years, and I'm at four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd believe that. Most new stuff at Brennan ends up being a bit useful and a bit annoying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I expected. Probably joke with the shift boss that the computer still can't fix a bent pick on the drum. Online, I don't post, I just read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get to year five, get the pay bump and get married. That's the whole plan, and in this picture it holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep the four-on, four-off. Use the AI app on my phone now and then to compare car insurance or check something, like I do now. Put every bit of overtime into the wedding fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, actually. I could stop half-listening to the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change at work, if AI were just a small helper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want it on the maintenance scheduling. Half our downtime is waiting on a part someone forgot to order. If a computer sorted that, I'd cut more metres and get more bonus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When's the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We're aiming for the autumn after next. Small, at Marta's uncle's farm, maybe sixty people and a barbecue. In this picture, that happens.

S0.say: He'd say it's about what he expected and joke that the computer still can't fix a bent pick on the cutting drum. He reads online but doesn't post.
S0.think: He sees this picture as letting his plan hold: reach year five for the pay rise and get married to his fiancée.
S0.do: Keeps working his four-on, four-off roster and uses an AI phone app now and then for small tasks. Puts all overtime into the wedding fund.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, able to stop half-listening to the news.
S0.quote: It means I get to year five, get the pay bump and get married. That's the whole plan, and in this picture it holds.
S0.fieldNote: Pedro's life is organised around two near-term goals: the year-five pay rise and his wedding. He sees AI as a possible small helper, especially for parts ordering. He's pragmatic and doesn't post opinions online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more like what I see coming, honestly. The other potash mine up north already has a miner you can run from the surface.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but fairly, you know. Give people training and time. I wouldn't be the guy shouting about it, but I wouldn't be the guy pretending it's not happening either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job changes rather than vanishes, at least for a few years. Someone still has to watch the machine, move the cables and deal with the ground. But I'd need to get onto the surface control side once it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for the first couple of people from our crew to try the surface control job and see how they find it. Then I'd put my hand up, probably within the year. Meanwhile I'd trim spending, cancel the sports channel, and keep putting overtime in the wedding fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but it's always there in the back of your head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for others first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first version of anything at Brennan is rubbish. When they brought in the new gas monitors, they went off every ten minutes for a month. I'd rather join on version two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the wedding change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. Maybe smaller, maybe a few less guests. Marta would say people still get married when things change, they just pick cheaper food.

S1.say: He'd say people need to adapt but fairly, with training and time; he wouldn't shout about it, but he wouldn't pretend it isn't happening.
S1.think: He believes his job will change rather than vanish for a few years, but he'd need to move onto the surface control side once it's proven.
S1.do: Waits for a couple of crewmates to try the surface control job, then applies within the year. Cancels the sports channel and keeps putting overtime into the wedding fund.
S1.feel: Uneasy, not scared, with the worry always in the back of his head.
S1.quote: The first version of anything at Brennan is rubbish.
S1.fieldNote: Pedro is a practical second-wave adopter, and he backs it with a real story about faulty gas monitors. He expects change, not loss, in this scenario. His fiancée's steady view helps him keep the wedding on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before the wedding would even happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government and the company to sort out something for workers, quickly. Not handouts forever, but something to bridge people. That's as political as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think my job's gone within a year of it arriving, and the surface control job too, if the AI can run the machine itself. And Marta's job, I don't know. Kids still need people, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd talk to Marta about postponing the wedding and keeping the money as our emergency fund. I'd take any shift I could while the mine still wanted people. I'd look at moving into something with people in it, like the hospital porters or the council, and I'd sign up for whatever support the government offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the roof creaking above you and you're not sure which bit's going to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would that conversation with Marta go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over dinner, probably, because that's when we talk about money. She'd be upset about the wedding, then she'd be the one with the spreadsheet by the end of the night. She's tougher than me about this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years of warning buy you, practically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to build a small cushion out of the wedding money, maybe a few months. Not time to train for anything new. You can't get a trade in two years when you're still working twelve-hour shifts.

S2.say: He'd say government and the company need to quickly arrange something for workers, not permanent handouts but a bridge.
S2.think: He expects both his job and the surface control job to vanish within a year of AGI arriving, and isn't sure his fiancée's school job is safe either.
S2.do: Talks to his fiancée about postponing the wedding and using the money as an emergency fund. Takes every available shift while the mine needs people, looks at jobs that involve people such as hospital porter or council work, and signs up for government support.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the roof creaking and not knowing which part will go.
S2.quote: Two years. That's before the wedding would even happen.
S2.fieldNote: Two years forces Pedro to give up the wedding plan he built everything around, at least for now. He wants a bridge, not ongoing handouts, which fits his centre outlook. He leans on his fiancée as the stronger planner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, I'd have time to get married and see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's use the time well. The company should be training people now, and the government should help small towns like Hollin get something else going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years gives me one decent move. I could get onto surface control early and then into maintenance, which might hang on longer. It's not safe, it's just a better seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the wedding as planned, but smaller, and keep half the fund as savings. I'd sign up for the surface control training in year one, once I'd seen it work for the first group. And I'd start using the AI app for study, because I'd need to learn electrical basics for the maintenance side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I was steering. That makes a difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep half the wedding fund. Does Marta agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd agree in this one, yes. She'd say we can have the big party when we're sure about work. She'd probably want the guest list down to forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would year five itself look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it goes right, I'd be on maintenance with a bit saved. If it goes wrong, at least we'd have had the wedding and a few months of money. Either way I'd know more than I do now.

S3.say: He'd say people should use the time well, with the company training workers now and government helping small towns build something else.
S3.think: He thinks five years gives him one decent move: surface control early, then maintenance, which might last longer. It's not safe, just a better seat.
S3.do: Holds a smaller wedding as planned and keeps half the fund as savings. Signs up for surface control training in year one once he's seen it work for others, and uses AI to study electrical basics for maintenance.
S3.feel: Anxious but feeling like he's steering, which helps.
S3.quote: It's not safe, it's just a better seat.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Pedro keep the wedding while still building a buffer, a balance he and his fiancée would agree on. He plans a two-step career move and is starting to use AI for study. He's realistic that neither step is truly safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long runway. I'd be thirty-seven with, I hope, a kid or two by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's plan instead of panicking. I'd want the company to start an apprenticeship scheme for maintenance and robotics, because they'll need people to look after the machines for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right for most of it. The worry is the end, when I might have a family relying on me and the machines can do the maintenance too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep mining and get married as planned. I'd start the electrical course part-time in year two, once I'd seen who from our crew got through it. And I'd try to save a steady hundred a fortnight once the wedding's paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It's a worry for later, and later is a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Would the ten-year picture change plans for a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might make us wait a year or two longer, so we've got some savings first. But I wouldn't want a robot deciding whether I have kids. That's the line for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I cancel my wedding. With ten, I have the wedding and a plan. That's the whole difference, really.

S4.say: He'd say there's time to plan instead of panicking and would want the company to start a maintenance and robotics apprenticeship scheme.
S4.think: He expects to be fine for most of the decade but worries about the end, when he might have a family relying on him and machines could do the maintenance too.
S4.do: Keeps mining and marries as planned in year one, starts a part-time electrical course in year two after seeing how crewmates fare, and saves a hundred a fortnight once the wedding is paid off.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, since the worry is a long way off.
S4.quote: But I wouldn't want a robot deciding whether I have kids. That's the line for me.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year picture lets Pedro keep his life plans almost intact while building skills gradually. He worries about the end of the decade, when he may have children. He drew a clear personal line on letting the change shape family decisions.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands right on top of the wedding and our first years together. What would help is a bridge payment while people change jobs, and the company running training before the machines come, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the women in mining towns. Marta's job feels safer than mine, but if the mine goes, the school loses kids too. It's all connected out here.

headlineQuote: With two years, I cancel my wedding. With ten, I have the wedding and a plan.
portrait: Pedro Quinn is a 27-year-old continuous miner operator at the Brennan potash mine, renting in Hollin with his fiancée Marta, a teaching assistant, with less than a month of savings and a wedding to pay for. He's practical and centrist, uses AI now and then, and likes to join new things on 'version two'. A plateau and steady change leave his plans mostly intact, though he'd move to surface control once it's proven. AGI in two years alarms him and forces the wedding to be postponed, while five and ten years let him marry and build towards maintenance work. He wants a bridge for workers, not permanent handouts.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would hit right as he's getting married and starting a life with his fiancée.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge payment while people change jobs, and the company running training before the machines arrive rather than after.
